CausalChain: Dietary & Environmental Factors + AI-guided Personalized Intervention -> Modulation of Gut Microbiota Composition (via targeted probiotic and dietary inputs using multi-omics feedback) -> Enhanced Conversion: Increased UDCA, Reduced DCA/LCA -> Selective Activation of Nuclear Receptors (FXR, VDR) over Pro-inflammatory Receptors (TGR5) -> Downregulation of NF-κB and MAPK Signaling -> Reduced Epithelial–Mesenchymal Transition and Tumor Proliferation
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a precision intervention strategy—incorporating AI-based personalized dietary and probiotic regimens informed by high-resolution metagenomic and metabolomic profiling—can modulate the gut microbiota to shift the bile acid pool toward a tumor-suppressive profile by increasing levels of UDCA relative to DCA and LCA. This bile acid profile shift is expected to reprogram bile acid receptor signaling by preferentially stimulating FXR and VDR, thus dampening NF-κB and MAPK inflammatory and proliferative pathways. Ultimately, this targeted modulation will reduce epithelial–mesenchymal transition and tumor cell proliferation in cancers such as colorectal and esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Abstract: This study proposes that leveraging contemporary multi-omics technologies and AI-driven personalized dietary and probiotic strategies can finely modulate the gut microbiota to favor the microbial conversion of primary bile acids into the tumor-suppressive metabolite ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) while reducing the formation of tumor-promoting bile acids deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA). The resulting altered bile acid profile is hypothesized to selectively enhance activation of nuclear receptors (FXR, VDR) over pro-inflammatory receptors such as TGR5, leading to attenuation of NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways. This, in turn, is expected to reduce epithelial–mesenchymal transition and proliferation in tumor cells, particularly in colorectal and esophageal adenocarcinoma. Advanced metagenomic, metabolomic, and receptor activity assays will be employed to capture individual variability, thereby facilitating a refined mechanistic understanding and enabling tailored intervention strategies.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that modulating the gut microbiota via dietary/probiotic interventions could shift bile acid composition towards increased UDCA and decreased DCA/LCA, thereby reprogramming receptor signaling and reducing cancer-related pathways. The new hypothesis retains this core causal chain but enhances it with modern technological capabilities. Specifically, it incorporates the use of high-resolution multi-omics (metagenomics and metabolomics) and AI-driven personalized intervention strategies to address individual variability and achieve a more controlled and measurable bile acid shift. Furthermore, the revised hypothesis explicitly identifies the modulation of nuclear receptors (FXR, VDR) and includes detailed downstream mechanistic outcomes (inhibition of NF-κB and MAPK signaling, reduced EMT) while acknowledging the complexity of host-microbiome interactions. Each original causal step is maintained and augmented: dietary/environmental inputs are now personalized, gut microbiota modulation is precisely monitored, bile acid conversion is quantitatively assessed, receptor signaling is specifically targeted, and the final anti-tumor outcomes are robustly linked to these earlier steps.
